asked: What are the content and format requirements for prescription drug labeling under the physician labeling rule?
answer:
The content and format requirements for prescription drug labeling under the physician labeling rule include a summary of essential scientific information needed for safe and effective use, that the labeling be informative, accurate, and neither promotional nor false or misleading, based on human experience when possible, with specific sections required in a defined order. Any reference in Highlights to information in the full prescribing information must be accompanied by an identifying number in parentheses indicating its location. If sections are omitted, the "Full Prescribing Information: Contents" section must be followed by an asterisk and the statement “* Sections or subsections omitted from the full prescribing information are not listed.” The labeling may include a "Product Title" section containing only specific product information required under § 201.80(a)(1)(i) through (a)(1)(iv), but the information required by those sections must also appear in the “Description” section, regardless of whether it appears in the Product Title. The requirement to reprint FDA-approved patient labeling at the end of prescription drug labeling or accompany it must be implemented no later than June 30, 2007. These requirements apply only to prescription drug products described in paragraph (b)(1) of this section under § 201.56(d), and for older prescription drug products not described in that category, the labeling requirements are governed by § 201.56(e). The specific information required under § 201.57(a), (b), and (c) must appear in designated headings and subheadings in a specified order [10]. The labeling must contain a summary of the essential scientific information needed for the safe and effective use of the drug [2]. The labeling must be informative and accurate and neither promotional in tone nor false or misleading in any particular, and must be updated when new information becomes available that causes it to become inaccurate, false, or misleading [3]. The labeling must be based whenever possible on data derived from human experience; no implied claims or suggestions of drug use may be made if there is inadequate evidence of safety or a lack of substantial evidence of effectiveness; conclusions based on animal data but necessary for safe and effective use in humans must be identified as such and included with human data [4]. Any reference in Highlights to information appearing in the full prescribing information must be accompanied by the identifying number (in parentheses) corresponding to the location of the information in the full prescribing information [11]. The heading “Full Prescribing Information: Contents” must be followed by an asterisk and the statement “* Sections or subsections omitted from the full prescribing information are not listed” if sections or subsections required under paragraph (d)(1) are omitted [12]. The information required by § 201.80(a)(1)(i) through (a)(1)(iv) must appear in the “Description” section of the labeling, whether or not it also appears in a “Product Title” [16]. The requirement to reprint any FDA-approved patient labeling at the end of prescription drug labeling or accompany the prescription drug labeling must be implemented no later than June 30, 2007 [17]. The labeling requirements for new and more recently approved prescription drug products apply only to prescription drug products described in paragraph (b)(1) of this section and must be implemented according to the schedule specified in paragraph (c) of this section [9]. The labeling requirements for older prescription drug products apply only to approved prescription drug products not described in paragraph (b)(1) of this section [14]. These provisions impose none on the format beyond what is required by the specific content and structural elements outlined.

asked: What are the requirements for the uniqueness and certification of electronic signatures?
answer:
The requirements for the uniqueness and certification of electronic signatures under 21 CFR 11.100 are as follows:

- Each electronic signature must be unique to one individual and shall not be reused by or reassigned to anyone else [1].  
- Before an organization establishes, assigns, certifies, or otherwise sanctions an individual's electronic signature, the organization shall verify the identity of the individual [2].  
- Persons using electronic signatures shall certify to the agency that the electronic signatures in their system, used on or after August 20, 1997, are intended to be the legally binding equivalent of traditional handwritten signatures [3].  
- The certification shall be signed with a traditional handwritten signature and submitted in electronic or paper form [4].  
- Persons using electronic signatures shall, upon agency request, provide additional certification or testimony that a specific electronic signature is the legally binding equivalent of the signer's handwritten signature [5].

These provisions impose no further restrictions on the use, format, or technical implementation of electronic signatures beyond uniqueness, identity verification, and the requirement for a handwritten signature to certify legal equivalence. The requirements are binding under 21 CFR 11.100, which is an authoritative regulation from the eCFR.

asked: How must net quantity of contents be declared?
answer:
The net quantity of contents must be declared on the label of a prescription or insulin-containing drug in package form, and the declaration shall be expressed in terms of weight, measure, numerical count, or a combination of numerical count and weight or measure [1]. For drugs in tablet, capsule, ampule, or other unit dosage forms, the quantity shall be expressed in terms of numerical count; for other dosage forms, it shall be in terms of weight if solid, semi-solid, or viscous, in terms of fluid measure if liquid, or in terms of volume measure if a designated medical gas or medically appropriate combination thereof is present [1].  

For gaseous contents in high-pressure containers, the net quantity shall be expressed in liters or cubic feet based on the filled pressure at 70 °F (21 °C) [3].  
For liquefied compressed gases in high-pressure containers, it shall be expressed in gaseous liters or by an appropriate net weight statement [4].  
For liquefied contents in portable cryogenic containers, it shall be expressed in gaseous liters, liquid liters (if identified as a liquid measure), gallons, or by an appropriate net weight statement at the time of fill [5].  
The declaration shall appear as a distinct item on the label and may be embossed for large volume parenterals [8].  
The declaration shall accurately reveal the quantity of drug in the package exclusive of wrappers and other material packed therewith [9].  
For liquid drugs, variations due to loss or gain of moisture during good distribution practice are recognized as reasonable, provided they do not exceed those specified by U.S. Pharmacopeia or National Formulary [11].  
In the case of solid drug in ampules or vials, the declaration shall express the accurate net weight; for liquid drugs intended for injection, it shall be considered to express the minimum quantity and any excess volume must comply with the excess volume prescribed by the National Formulary or U.S. Pharmacopeia [11].  
A drug labeled “sample”, “physician's sample”, or substantially similar with contents not exceeding 8 grams is exempt from this requirement [12].

asked: When is an Investigational Device Exemption required and what are the significant risk criteria?
answer:
An Investigational Device Exemption (IDE) for treatment use is required when a device is intended to treat or diagnose a serious or immediately life-threatening disease or condition in patients for whom no comparable or satisfactory alternative device or therapy is available, and the device is under investigation in a controlled clinical trial for the same use under an approved IDE, or such trials have been completed. The significant risk criteria that may lead to disapproval or withdrawal of a treatment IDE include: when the available scientific evidence fails to provide a reasonable basis for concluding that the device would not expose patients to an unreasonable and significant additional risk of illness or injury; when there is reasonable evidence that the treatment use is impeding enrollment in, or otherwise interfering with, the conduct or completion of a controlled investigation; when a comparable device or therapy becomes available to treat or diagnose the same indication in the same patient population; when approval of the IDE for the controlled clinical investigation has been withdrawn; and when the clinical investigator(s) named in the treatment IDE are not qualified by reason of their scientific training and/or experience to use the device for the intended treatment use. Treatment use is permitted only if the sponsor is actively pursuing marketing approval/clearance with due diligence [5].

A treatment IDE is required when:  
- The device is intended to treat or diagnose a serious or immediately life-threatening disease or condition [3].  
- The device is under investigation in a controlled clinical trial for the same use under an approved IDE, or such trials have been completed [4].  
- The sponsor of the investigation is actively pursuing marketing approval/clearance of the investigational device with due diligence [5].

The significant risk criteria that may lead to disapproval or withdrawal of a treatment IDE include:  
- When the available scientific evidence fails to provide a reasonable basis for concluding that the device would not expose patients to an unreasonable and significant additional risk of illness or injury [16].  
- When there is reasonable evidence that the treatment use is impeding enrollment in, or otherwise interfering with, the conduct or completion of a controlled investigation [17].  
- When a comparable device or therapy becomes available to treat or diagnose the same indication in the same patient population [18].  
- When approval of the IDE for the controlled clinical investigation has been withdrawn [19].  
- When the clinical investigator(s) named in the treatment IDE are not qualified by reason of their scientific training and/or experience to use the device for the intended treatment use [20].

A written protocol describing the treatment use, patient selection criteria, and the intended use of the device is required under §812.36(c)(1)(ii) [8].  
An explanation of the rationale for use of the device, including either a list of available regimens that ordinarily should be tried before using the investigational device or an explanation of why the use of the investigational device is preferable to available marketed treatments, is required under §812.36(c)(1)(iii) [9].  
A description of clinical procedures, laboratory tests, or other measures to evaluate the effects of the device and minimize risk is required under §812.36(c)(1)(iv) [10].  
Instructions for use for the device and all other labeling as required under §812.5(a) and (b) are required under §812.36(c)(1)(vi) [11].  
Treatment use is conditioned upon compliance with safeguards, including informed consent and institutional review board oversight, as specified in §812.36(e) [21].

asked: What is required by the stability testing regulation?
answer:
The stability testing regulation requires a written testing program to assess the stability characteristics of drug products, which must include sample size and test intervals based on statistical criteria, storage conditions for samples retained for testing, reliable and meaningful specific test methods, testing in the same container-closure system as marketed, testing of reconstituted products at dispensing and after reconstitution, and a written assessment of stability based on testing or examination for ingredient compatibility and marketing experience to indicate no degradation during normal use. The evaluation must be conducted using the same container-closure system as that used in marketing, and an adequate number of batches must be tested to determine an appropriate expiration date with records maintained; accelerated studies may support a tentative expiration date if full shelf life studies are not available, but such a tentative date beyond actual shelf life data requires further stability testing until verified or the expiration date is determined. These provisions impose none on other aspects not specified.

- A written testing program designed to assess the stability characteristics of drug products must be established and followed, including sample size and test intervals based on statistical criteria for each attribute examined to assure valid estimates of stability [1].  
- Storage conditions for samples retained for testing must be specified in the written program [3].  
- Reliable, meaningful, and specific test methods must be used for evaluating stability [4].  
- Testing of drug products must occur in the same container-closure system as that in which the product is marketed [5].  
- Testing of drug products for reconstitution at the time of dispensing (as directed in labeling) and after reconstitution must be conducted [6].  
- There shall be a written assessment of stability based at least on testing or examination of the drug product for compatibility of ingredients, and based on marketing experience to indicate no degradation during normal or expected use [9].  
- Evaluation of stability must be based on the same container-closure system in which the drug product is being marketed [10].  

The available regulatory sources do not provide enough information to answer this.

asked: A product is packaged in a container that holds between 200 and 300 percent of the RACC. How must the Nutrition Facts be presented?
answer:
A product packaged in a container that holds between 200 and 300 percent of the Reference Amount Customarily Consumed Per Eating Occasion (RACC) must provide an additional column within the Nutrition Facts label that lists the quantitative amounts and percent Daily Values for the entire package, as well as a column listing the quantitative amounts and percent Daily Values for a serving that is less than the entire package (i.e., the serving size derived from the reference amount). This requirement applies specifically to individually packaged products containing at least 200 percent and up to and including 300 percent of the applicable RACC. [5]

The provision requires that such products provide an additional column for the entire package content, in addition to a column for a serving size derived from the reference amount. [5]  
This requirement does not apply if the product is intended solely for weight control and available only through a weight-control program; however, such products must still follow the serving size determination rules based on Reference Amounts Customarily Consumed Per Eating Occasion. [2]  
For individually packaged products containing less than 200 percent of the RACC, the entire content is considered a single-serving container and must be labeled as one serving. [4]  
The requirement to provide an additional column for the entire package and per serving applies only when the product contains at least 200 percent and up to 300 percent of the RACC. [5]  
No other specific nutrient or food component declarations are required beyond those specified in §101.9(c), which governs the format and content of nutrition information, including total carbohydrate calculation by subtraction of crude protein, total fat, moisture, and ash from the total weight of the food. [7]  

The statement “Not a significant source of added sugars” shall be placed at the bottom of the table of nutrient values in the same type size if no added sugars content is declared due to less than 1 gram per serving and no claims are made about sweeteners, sugars, or sugar alcohols. [8]  

The available regulatory sources do not provide enough information to answer whether any specific format for the serving size declaration (e.g., household measure) is required beyond what is specified in §101.9(b)(6). [4]

This requirement applies specifically to individually packaged products containing at least 200 percent and up to and including 300 percent of the applicable RACC. [5]

The provision requires that such products provide an additional column for the entire package content, in addition to a column for a serving size derived from the reference amount. [5]  
This requirement does not apply if the product is intended solely for weight control and available only through a weight-control program; however, such products must still follow the serving size determination rules based on Reference Amounts Customarily Consumed Per Eating Occasion. [2]  
For individually packaged products containing less than 200 percent of the RACC, the entire content is considered a single-serving container and must be labeled as one serving. [4]  
The requirement to provide an additional column for the entire package and per serving applies only when the product contains at least 200 percent and up to 300 percent of the RACC. [5]  
No other specific nutrient or food component declarations are required beyond those specified in §101.9(c), which governs the format and content of nutrition information, including total carbohydrate calculation by subtraction of crude protein, total fat, moisture, and ash from the total weight of the food. asked: What requirements apply to equipment and utensils under Part 117 Subpart B?
answer:
Equipment and utensils used in manufacturing, processing, packing, or holding food must be designed and constructed so as to be adequately cleanable and must be maintained to protect against allergen cross-contact and contamination [1]. Equipment and utensils must be designed, constructed, and used appropriately to avoid the adulteration of food with lubricants, fuel, metal fragments, contaminated water, or any other contaminants [2]. Equipment must be installed so as to facilitate the cleaning and maintenance of the equipment and of adjacent spaces [3]. Cleaning compounds and sanitizing agents used in cleaning and sanitizing procedures must be free from undesirable microorganisms and must be safe and adequate under the conditions of use; compliance with this requirement must be verified by any effective means, including purchase of these substances under a letter of guarantee or certification or examination of these substances for contamination [6]. The water supply must be adequate for the operations intended and must be derived from an adequate source; any water that contacts food, food-contact surfaces, or food-packaging materials must be safe and of adequate sanitary quality [8]. Plumbing must be of adequate size and design and adequately installed and maintained to facilitate cleaning and maintenance [9].

asked: What sanitation requirements apply to plant and grounds under Part 117 Subpart B?
answer:
Sanitation requirements for plant and grounds under Part 117 Subpart B include maintaining the grounds in a condition that protects against food contamination by properly storing equipment, removing litter and waste, cutting weeds or grass within the immediate vicinity of the plant to prevent pest attraction, breeding, or harborage, and maintaining roads, yards, and parking lots so they do not constitute a source of contamination where food is exposed [1].

The following sanitation requirements apply to plant and grounds under 21 CFR part 117:

- Grounds must be kept in a condition that will protect against the contamination of food; methods for adequate maintenance must include properly storing equipment, removing litter and waste, and cutting weeds or grass within the immediate vicinity of the plant if such conditions may constitute an attractant, breeding place, or harborage for pests [1].

- Grounds must be maintained so that roads, yards, and parking lots do not constitute a source of contamination in areas where food is exposed [1].

- Cleaning compounds and sanitizing agents used in cleaning and sanitizing procedures must be free from undesirable microorganisms and must be safe and adequate under the conditions of use; compliance with this requirement must be verified by any effective means, including purchase of these substances under a letter of guarantee or certification or examination of these substances for contamination [6].

- The water supply must be adequate for the operations intended and must be derived from an adequate source; any water that contacts food, food-contact surfaces, or food-packaging materials must be safe and of adequate sanitary quality [8].

- Plumbing must be of adequate size and design and adequately installed and maintained to ensure effective operation in areas where food is processed, equipment is cleaned, or employee sanitary facilities are used [9].

These provisions impose none on the frequency, specific methods, or types of sanitation activities beyond what is specified; they do not establish timeframes, specific inspection frequencies, or defined procedures for implementation beyond the general conditions described. The requirements depend on "as appropriate" to the nature of the preventive control and its role in the facility's food safety system [21], [22], [23].

asked: What must a supply-chain program include under Part 117 Subpart G?
answer:
A supply-chain program under Part 117 Subpart G must include using approved suppliers as required by § 117.420 and determining appropriate supplier verification activities, including the frequency of conducting such activities, as required by § 117.425. The receiving facility must also document these elements in records as applicable to its supply-chain program [6]. 

21 CFR 117.410(a)(1) – The supply-chain program must include using approved suppliers as required by § 117.420 [2]. 
 
21 CFR 117.475(c) – The receiving facility must document the following in records as applicable to its supply-chain program [6]. 
21 CFR 117.475(a) – The records documenting the supply-chain program are subject to the requirements of subpart F of this part [4]. 
 

Note: The requirement to document specific elements applies "as applicable" to its supply-chain program, indicating that documentation is not required for all cases but only when relevant [6].

asked: Which provisions of Part 820 are FDA supplements to the incorporated standard rather than incorporation by reference?
answer:
The provisions of 21 CFR part 820 that are FDA supplements to incorporated standards rather than incorporation by reference include those that add specific record-keeping and procedural requirements beyond the referenced ISO standards, as explicitly stated in the text.

The requirement that a manufacturer shall maintain records of the review, evaluation, and investigation for any complaints involving the possible failure of a device, labeling, or packaging to meet any of its specifications is a supplement to ISO 13485 Clause 8.2.2, as specified in §820.35(a). [5]  
The requirement that the name of the device must be included in records related to complaints is specified in §820.35(a)(1) and is a direct addition not present in ISO 13485. [6]  
The requirement for manufacturers to document and maintain procedures ensuring the integrity, inspection, storage, and operations for labeling and packaging during customary conditions of processing, storage, handling, distribution, and as appropriate, use of the device is a supplemental requirement added by FDA beyond ISO 13485 Clause 7.5.1. [10]  
The definition of "batch or lot" in §820.3(a) is provided for the purposes of this part and applies to the context of devices, as stated in §820.3(a). [9]  
The exception in §820.3 that the definitions from ISO 13485 and Clause 3 of ISO 9000 apply "except as specified in paragraph (b) of this section" indicates that certain terms are modified by FDA-specific language for use in device regulation. [7]

asked: Which products are subject to FDA tobacco authority under the deeming rule, and what does Part 1100 address?
answer:
Products subject to FDA tobacco authority under the deeming rule are all products that meet the definition of a tobacco product under section 201(rr) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, except accessories of such other tobacco products. Part 1100 addresses the scope and requirements of FDA's authority over tobacco products under chapter IX of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, including the deeming of such products as subject to regulation when they meet the definition of a tobacco product, except for accessories and certain products intended for medical use [2].

The following provisions address specific aspects of the deeming rule:

- Products that are intended for use in the diagnosis of disease or other conditions, or in the cure, mitigation, treatment, or prevention of disease—including use in curing or treating nicotine addiction, relapse prevention, or relief of nicotine withdrawal symptoms—are excluded from tobacco regulation and subject to drug, device, or combination product regulation [4].

- Products that are intended to affect the structure or any function of the body in a way different from effects related to nicotine commonly and legally claimed in cigarette and smokeless tobacco marketing prior to March 21, 2000, are excluded from tobacco regulation and subject to drug, device, or combination product regulation [5].

These provisions establish that certain products intended for medical purposes—specifically those involving diagnosis, treatment of disease, or effects beyond nicotine-related functions—are not considered tobacco products under section 201(rr) and thus fall outside the scope of the deeming rule. The deeming rule applies to all other tobacco products meeting the statutory definition, except accessories [1].
